Baghdad History for Sleep 🌙 The Night Paper Changed the World

About 1 hour 53 min · Released Wed 4 Nov 2026 · Updated 5 Nov 2026 · narrated slowly for sleep

Watch on YouTube Listen on YouTube Music

Baghdad history for sleep: a calm night in 9th-century Baghdad, when paper was still fairly new in the city, with a translator, reed pens, ink and a Greek book.

Brown paper, a reed pen and a Greek book being turned into Arabic. This bedtime story for grown-ups spends nearly two slow hours in a hired workroom on the west bank of the Tigris, on a quiet night in the 850s, with a translator, a copyist and a messenger. Told in calming history narration, it follows the paper itself: where it came from, why officials trusted a mark that soaked in, and how a sheet becomes a copied book. It is relaxing bedtime history, careful about what the sources say.

🌙 No mid-video ads, nothing to wake you.

It is a night in Baghdad, more than eleven hundred years ago. A lamp burns low over a Greek book and a fresh sheet of paper, and someone is turning one language into another, one careful line at a time.

Tonight we stay in that workroom and its streets: brown paper that takes a reed pen, one careful line of Greek turned into Arabic, a messenger carrying a patron's request, a sum on a board of dust, the stationers' row shut for the night, cakes of ink ground on a stone, and the Tigris before morning. The caliph's library, called the House of Wisdom, stays a name in the background: historians still debate what it was, and we do not describe its rooms.

This is a quiet bedtime documentary, narrated slowly to help you relax and drift off to sleep. No loud sounds, no sudden changes: just a soft voice, slow images, and the river in the dark.

About this sleep story

About 1 hour 53 min, narrated slowly for sleep, with no ad breaks. Made as history to fall asleep to: it's fine to drift off partway, and the chapters below let you find your place again.

Paper is the quiet star of this night. Baghdad, the Tigris, the paper and the caliph's library are real, and so are the scholars named in the old catalogues. Dawud, Nafi, Harith, Layla and Ibrahim are imagined, but people like them lived and worked here. Historians still discuss what the House of Wisdom was; where sources disagree, the narration says so.

Sources

Researched and written for this channel from these sources. Where historians disagree, the narration says so.

  • Dimitri Gutas, Greek Thought, Arabic Culture (Routledge, 1998)
  • Ibn al-Nadim, The Fihrist, tr. Bayard Dodge (Columbia University Press, 1970)
  • The Abbasid House of Wisdom: Between Myth and Reality (Routledge)
  • Jonathan M. Bloom, Paper Before Print (Yale, 2001); "Revolution by the Ream", Saudi Aramco World (1999)
  • Biographical Encyclopedia of Astronomers (Springer, 2007): al-Ma'mun, al-Khwarizmi, Banu Musa
  • MacTutor History of Mathematics: Hunayn ibn Ishaq, Thabit ibn Qurra
  • Encyclopaedia Iranica: "Qalam (pen)", "Calligraphy VI", "Bibliographies and catalogues ii"
  • al-Ya'qubi, Kitab al-Buldan (c. 891), via Textbook of Architecture, "Early Baghdad"
  • Smarthistory, "The founding of Baghdad"
